# Diagnosing Water Intrusion in a 2002 Mazda ProtÃ©gÃ©

A damp spot on the back passenger floor of a 2002 Mazda ProtÃ©gÃ© is rarely just "rain." While weather seals can fail, the progression from a rear wet floor to soaked front sections and eventually into the trunk suggests a systemic drainage failure or a specific breach in the cabin air handling system. The presence of vapor on the glass and a growing odor indicates active moisture migration, which, if left untreated, will lead to mold growth within the carpet padding and structural corrosion of the floor pan.

The most common culprit in vehicles of this era is the clogged sunroof or rear window drain tubes. These tubes are designed to channel water away from the roof cavity into the wheel wells. Over time, leaves, dirt, and debris accumulate inside these narrow channels, creating a dam. When it rains, the water level rises behind this blockage. Once the capacity of the tray beneath the roof lining is exceeded, gravity takes over, and water spills out through the weakest point in the seal: the floor carpet on the passenger side. This explains why the rear floor is affected first; the drain outlets often terminate near the kick panels or under the carpet edge.

To verify this hypothesis without fully disassembling the interior, you can perform a targeted flood test. Have an assistant stand outside with a garden hose and spray water directly into the sunroof channels and rear window weep holes while you monitor the interior. Use a flashlight to inspect the area around the passenger side footwell from below. If water begins to seep out of the carpet trim or floor lining, you have confirmed a clogged drain. The solution is not to vacuum the water out repeatedly, as this only masks the issue and pushes mold deeper into the padding. Instead, you must clear the blockage using a flexible drain cleaner or compressed air from the exterior access points.

If the sunroof drains are cleared and the problem persists, the leak likely originates from the cabin air filter housing. On many Mazda models of this generation, the HVAC box is located under the dashboard on the passenger side. If the seal around the fresh air intake ducting degrades or if the firewall gasket fails, water can enter through the vents when the A/C is running or during heavy rain. This scenario explains why the moisture appears in both the front and rear passenger areas; once it enters the HVAC box, it spreads across the entire floor pan via capillary action in the carpet backing.

Another possibility involves the door sill seals or the quarter panel pinch welds. Inspect the rubber weatherstripping along the passenger side doors and rear quarter panels. If these are brittle or torn, water flowing down the exterior of the car will track directly into the cabin. This is a more direct intrusion path than the roof drains but often harder to spot visually from the inside.

Removing the carpet and padding is the only definitive way to assess the extent of the damage. Once removed, inspect the metal floor pan for rust spots. If the carpet has been soaked for weeks, the foam padding will likely be saturated with stagnant water and microbial growth. In this case, replacing the pad is cheaper than attempting to dry it out, as you cannot fully sanitize wet organic material without heat that might warp the carpet backing.

Before tackling the mechanical repairs, ensure your cabin air filter is clean or replaced. A clogged filter can restrict airflow, causing the evaporator core to freeze slightly and then thaw, potentially releasing excess condensation into the system. While this usually causes a smell rather than a flood, it contributes to the overall moisture environment.

If you are comfortable working on automotive HVAC systems, consider checking the drain tube at the bottom of the evaporator case. If this drains into the passenger footwell instead of exiting near the bumper, water will accumulate inside the cabin regardless of external rain. Clearing these specific pathways is a critical maintenance step often overlooked until significant damage occurs.
